items.title: Apple now assembles 25% of iPhones in India

items.description: Apple assembled roughly 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, a 53 percent jump from 36 million the year before, according to a Bloomberg report published Monday. The milestone means that about one in every four iPhones produced worldwide is now made in India, as the company accelerates efforts to diversify manufacturing away from China amid persistent U.S. tariff pressures.[1]

items.title: ALMA detects high methanol levels in interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS

featured_image.name: An interstellar comet packed with alcohol? What ALMA found in 3I/ATLAS

items.description:
Astronomers using one of the world's most powerful radio telescope arrays have discovered that the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS contains extraordinary levels of methanol compared with hydrogen cyanide, a chemical fingerprint unlike nearly anything observed in comets born in our own solar system. The findings, announced by the ALMA Observatory on March 8, suggest the comet formed under conditions vastly different from those that shaped familiar solar system objects.[1]

The research team, led by Nathan Roth, a professor at American University, used ALMA's Atacama Compact Array in Chile to observe 3I/ATLAS multiple times in late 2025 as it drew closer to the Sun. On two separate observation dates, they measured methanol-to-hydrogen cyanide ratios of roughly 70 and 120, placing the comet among the most methanol-rich ever studied.[2][1]

"Observing 3I/ATLAS is like taking a fingerprint from another solar system," Roth said. "The details reveal what it's made of, and it's bursting with methanol in a way we just don't usually see in comets in our own solar system."[1]

items.title: Engineers hide data in heat radiation using 'negative light'

featured_image.name: New 'negative light' technology hides data transfers in ...

items.description: Engineers at UNSW Sydney and Monash University have built a communication system that conceals data transmissions within natural heat radiation, making them virtually undetectable. The technology, described in a paper published March 4 in the Nature Publishing Group journal Light: Science and Applications, exploits a phenomenon called "negative luminescence" to create what the researchers call "thermoradiative signatureless communication."[1][2]

items.title: Sydney researchers build AI chip that computes at speed of light

featured_image.name: Photonic chip that 'fits together like Lego' opens door to ...

items.description: Researchers at the University of Sydney have built a prototype artificial intelligence chip that processes data using light instead of electricity, performing calculations at the speed of light on a picosecond timescale — trillionths of a second. The nanophotonic chip, described in a study published in Nature Communications, points toward a future of faster and more energy-efficient AI hardware.[1][2]

items.title: Macron, IAEA chief open nuclear energy summit in Paris

featured_image.name: Macron to outline France's contribution to Europe's nuclear ...

items.description:
World leaders are convening in Paris on Monday for the second Nuclear Energy Summit, an event hosted by the French government in cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency to promote the expansion of civilian nuclear power at a moment of acute energy insecurity and escalating conflict in the Middle East.

French President Emmanuel Macron and IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi opened the summit, with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also delivering remarks. The gathering brings together heads of state and government, leaders of international organizations and financial institutions, and industry experts to discuss nuclear energy's role in decarbonization, energy security, and meeting surging electricity demand.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Oil's surge to $120 renews global push for clean energy

featured_image.name: Instant View: Oil surges 20% as Iran war fuels supply fears | Reuters

items.description:
The U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, now entering its second week, has knocked out roughly a fifth of the world's oil and natural gas supply and sent energy prices surging — and the crisis is renewing calls from governments, investors, and analysts to accelerate the transition to domestically produced renewable energy.

Since the strikes began on February 28, Iran has retaliated by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, attacking energy infrastructure across the Persian Gulf, and forcing production stoppages from Qatar to Iraq. Brent crude has surged from about $73 before the conflict to around $120 on Monday, according to Reuters, rattling markets worldwide. QatarEnergy declared force majeure on its liquefied natural gas exports — representing about 20 percent of global LNG supply — after Iranian drone strikes, and may need at least a month to restore output.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Cortical Labs unveils data centers powered by human brain cells

featured_image.name: Human Brain Cells Run New Data Centers in Singapore ...

items.description: Australian biotech startup Cortical Labs announced Tuesday that it has unveiled the world's first biological data center in Melbourne and is building a second facility in Singapore, both powered not by conventional computer chips but by lab-grown human brain cells. The move represents a novel attempt to address the surging energy demands of artificial intelligence by turning to biology for computing power.

items.title: Oil nears $120 a barrel as Iran war sparks historic market surge

featured_image.name: Oil supertanker rates hit all-time high as Iran pledges to close the Strait of Hormuz

items.description: Oil prices surged past $100 a barrel on Monday for the first time since 2022, as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran entered its second week with no signs of abating. Brent crude briefly touched nearly $120 per barrel before settling around $105, marking what Reuters described as the benchmark's largest single-day gain ever in both percentage and absolute terms. The spike sent shockwaves through global financial markets, with Asian stocks plunging and European equities hitting their lowest levels in more than two months.[1][2]

items.title: Oil tops $100 a barrel as Iran war chokes global supply

featured_image.name: Oil prices surge, but no panic yet, as Iran war continues - NPR

items.description:
The price of crude oil surged past $100 a barrel on Monday as the U.S.-led war in Iran entered its second week, sending gasoline prices sharply higher for American consumers and raising fears of a prolonged energy crisis rooted in the near-total closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude climbed to $103.74 per barrel on March 9, up nearly 12% from the previous trading day alone and roughly 50% higher than a month ago, according to Trading Economics. WTI crude oil futures spiked as high as $108 per barrel after Sunday evening's futures open, a historic jump from $72 at the start of the prior week. The national average for a gallon of regular gasoline reached $3.47 on Monday, according to AAA, up from $2.99 just one week earlier — a rise of about 48 cents in seven days.[1][2][3][4]
